messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was forty-eight when it happened—a Thursday night after a quartet rehearsal at a downtown arts center. He'd been loading equipment into his van when a man he recognized vaguely from the building's security staff approached him in the parking garage. The man had seemed friendly at first, asking about the music, complimenting Marcus's cello playing. Within minutes, Marcus found himself pinned against the concrete wall, his protests met with a hand over his mouth and threats delivered in a low, deliberate voice. The assault lasted perhaps ten minutes, though Marcus has never been certain of the duration. What remains crystalline is the smell—an overwhelming cologne, cheap and cloying, that the man wore—and the sudden, violent movements of his attacker's hands. What has dissolved is almost everything else: the exact sequence of events, what was said after the initial threats, whether anyone had been nearby. Some moments stand in sharp relief—the cold wall against his spine, the man's breathing—while others have simply vanished, leaving Marcus with a fragmented, incoherent account of his own trauma that he cannot even narrate to himself with any sense of completeness or order.

In the eight years since, Marcus has constructed his life around an ever-narrowing geography of safety. He feels secure only at home, in his music studio, and in the homes of his wife and one trusted friend. Anywhere else—the grocery store, a coffee shop, a concert hall—triggers a vigilance so acute that he cannot relax. Any sudden movement from another person sends him into an immediate state of heightened alert, his body bracing as if the assault might recur at any moment. The sight of blood on a television screen or in the news, the sound of violence in a film, the glimpse of a police officer or security guard in uniform—all of these penetrate his carefully constructed sense of safety and resurrect the threat he has come to believe is constant and omnipresent. The cologne that his attacker wore has become a phantom threat; whenever he encounters a similar scent, his nervous system floods with panic and the fragmented memories of that night surge forward, incomplete and terrifying.

Over the years, Marcus has developed strategies to manage the chaos, though they have come at considerable cost. Because the fragmented, intrusive memories feel unbearable—arriving without warning and leaving him disoriented—he has learned to suppress them the moment they begin to surface. The instant he feels a memory emerging, he consciously pushes it away, refusing to follow the thread, cutting it off before it can take fuller shape. This suppression has become so automatic that he is no longer fully aware he is doing it; the memories remain fragmented, never coalescing into a narrative he could work through or integrate. Alongside this, Marcus has come to believe that anger is dangerous—that if he allows himself to feel the rage that sometimes wells up in response to his trauma, he will lose control entirely. He has made a rule for himself: he will never permit anger to surface, let alone express it. This rigid suppression of a natural response to violation has left him emotionally constricted, prone to sudden, unpredictable outbursts of irritability that confuse even him. The anger he refuses to acknowledge emerges instead as explosive reactions to minor frustrations—a wrong note during practice, a delayed email from a colleague—leaving him exhausted and ashamed.

The threat he perceives everywhere has also reshaped his relationships and his approach to authority. He avoids being around people in uniform or positions of authority, convinced that such figures represent danger or judgment. Over time, he has also withdrawn from the social contacts he maintained before the assault—former bandmates, colleagues from the arts center, musicians he used to collaborate with. When he encounters one of them, the encounter feels contaminated by the memory of who he was before, and he experiences a surge of discomfort that he cannot quite name. He has simply begun declining invitations, taking fewer gigs, isolating himself further. His wife, Elena, has watched this contraction with growing concern. Marcus's work as a freelance cellist has dried up considerably; he turns down ensemble work and teaching opportunities, claiming scheduling conflicts. What he cannot tell her is that the prospect of being in a room full of people, or of being observed while he plays, feels unbearable—that the threat monitoring that has become his constant companion makes public performance feel impossible.

The suppression of his anger and his refusal to fully engage with his fragmented memories have created a vicious loop. By refusing to feel or express anger, Marcus denies himself any release or processing of the violation he experienced. The unprocessed rage then fuels his irritability, which in turn makes him more vigilant to perceived threats—a colleague's raised voice, a sudden gesture—all of which he interprets through the lens of danger. This heightened threat perception then triggers more memories, which he immediately suppresses, which intensifies the anger he refuses to acknowledge. The fragmented memories remain fragmented, never integrated into a coherent narrative, which means the triggers retain their full power. A whiff of cologne can derail his entire week. The sight of someone in a security uniform can send him spiraling into avoidance of the places he would otherwise need to go.

Marcus is fifty-six now, and he has come to therapy because Elena issued an ultimatum. She loves him, she said, but she cannot watch him disappear. He has agreed to seek help, though he is terrified of what might happen if he stops pushing the memories away, if he allows himself to feel the anger he has spent years denying, if he has to confront the fragmented pieces of that night and somehow make them whole. What he wants most is to feel safe again, to walk into a room without scanning for threats, to play music in front of an audience without his hands shaking. What he fears most is that if he stops controlling himself—if he stops suppressing, stops avoiding, stops bracing—he will shatter entirely.
